To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the Opitz syndrome gene MID1 regulates the mTORC1 pathway by controlling the formation of the mTORC complex, thereby controlling cell size and cap-dependent translation.
the MID1/OPitz BBB/G syndrome E3 ubiquitin ligase regulates the mTORC1 kinase complex and that this regulation is required for normal cell growth and size.
mutations in the MID1 E3 ligase lead to dysregulated mTORC1 activity and that mTORC 1 signaling is a key pathway in the development of Opitz syndrome.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification and characterization of novel pathways regulated by the Opitz Syndrome protein MID1 and the elucidation of its function in the development of ventral midline organs.
the identification and characterization of novel molecular pathways that are affected in OS.
the molecular mechanisms of the Opitz BBB/G syndromes, which are a group of congenital malformation syndromes with a wide spectrum of phenotypic manifestations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Opitz Syndrome (OS) is a genetic disorder caused by mutations in the gene that encodes the protein MID1.
the MID1/ PP2A axis is a novel and important regulator of mTORC2 signaling, which is essential for cell growth, cell size control, cell proliferation and protein synthesis.
mTORC 1 signaling is a downstream pathway that is regulated by the MID 1 PP 2A axis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
MID1 is required to regulate mTORC1 activity.
MID1 is a key regulator of the mTORC1 pathway.
the MID1 protein functions as an E3 ubiquitin ligase targeting the PP2A-C catalytic subunit for degradation, and that this pathway controls mTORC1 activity and downstream cellular events.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the MID1 E3 ubiquitin ligase regulates mTORC1 activity by controlling the levels of the mTOR complex component Raptor.
the Opitz syndrome (OS) protein MID1 controls mTORC1 activity.
the Opitz BBB/G Syndrome (OS), an X-linked congenital malformation syndrome, is caused by mutations in the MID1 protein, and that this protein is involved in the regulation of mTORC signaling.
